comments.text: What should you do? Lie. I’ve been on both sides of the job search in the past couple years. Like you, absolutely no luck with cold applications. On the hiring side, opening a position got me a thousand of applications per day, all ChatGPT’d resumes from monkeys who likely couldn’t engineer their way out of a wet paper bag (beyond just grossly lying about experience, there’s also actual remote work fraud, either from the “overemployed” crowd if not outright scams or North Koreans). Unfortunately, in all that mess I’m sure there were really good legitimate candidates but there is no way for me to tell without talking to them, which was impossible considering the sheer scale of the spam onslaught. My advice is twofold. 1) Lie - nobody legitimate would actually care about your 2-year career gap, yet due to the scale of the spam, automated tools have to be used to cull the incoming firehose, and those unfortunately do care. So lie and extend your last job, or make up some consulting gig, or whatever floats your boat. As long as you can walk the talk during the interview, you are good. As a hirer I couldn’t care less (and wouldn’t even have any reason to dig too deep) if you are otherwise competent and able to talk about your work and can demonstrate you are a good developer and not just a dumbass vibecoder ticket-mover. In the sea of shit we’re currently swimming, even a candidate I know is lying is fine as long as they’re otherwise competent. 2) cold applications are pretty much dead due to the aforementioned spam problem. So my recommendation is to polish up your LinkedIn (you do have 15 YOE of real experience after all, with people you worked with and stuff) and then reach out to strategic people at prospective companies. Don’t even ask for a job to begin with - offer consultancy, etc (the danger of asking for a job straight away is that they shut down the conversation and redirect you to the cold application page - a dead end). The point is to have a conversation with a human, to demonstrate you are a real person and not an idiot with a spambot. If the conversation goes anywhere you’ve just fast-tracked the whole bullshit application process (you might still be asked to submit it, but at that point it’s merely a formality and you’ve already got a contact that will follow up internally to make sure your application goes somewhere). Also, if you’re at the stage where you’re considering a blue-collar job, target companies that could potentially benefit from IT skills or where you can use them to make your job easier if not make their job easier and get promoted that way. In a sense, you’re using the blue-collar job merely as a foot in the door to be able to show up and talk to people. While it’s unlikely this would yield good pay right away (and potentially not ever), it’s a good way to build connections and potentially get something done (remember that those companies don’t get IT people and might be stuck with a shitty MSP handling their IT. Having someone “good with computers” internally would be a godsend for them and a win-win situation). Ultimately in the age of AI-assisted spam and no consequences for fraud, the hardest part is getting a respectable human connection. Lie (within reason) if you have to, to achieve that, then be yourself, and you’ll get somewhere. Good luck!

posts.title: This Industrial Revolution Belongs to the Builders
posts.text: You've heard AI = Labor. Therefore Labor -> 0. Some people think this means that only asset owners, people with lots of capital, will come out ahead. They're wrong. Because as a builder/founder, you create value. Capital must capture some of this value to have a return. The reason founders primarily need capital is to pay for labor (either employees or supplier overhead). So this means that Capital ~= Labor. But that's a problem for the "owners of capital will own everything" narrative, because now we have: AI = Labor = Capital -> 0 In practice this will happen slowly as builders need less and less capital to build, capital will increasingly struggle to capture value created by builders. Counterintuitively this means valuations will climb dramatically reflecting capital paying more and more to capture less and less value from builders. As disruption accelerates, volatility increases while broader market wide returns start to stagnate. The net will be a wholesale wealth and power transfer from capital holders to builders/founders, on the magnitude of what happened between the aristocracy and the capitalist class in the earlier industrial revolutions. It's already started, companies are raising later and at higher valuations. Most people accept that if superintelligence were created, capital would be useless, but what they often don't realize is that a class of builders armed with AI is already creating a distributed superintelligence that will have the same effect. Interested if anyone else shares this perspective.

posts.title: Ask HN: Should Uber Ratings Decay over Time?
posts.text: I’ve been thinking about how platforms like Uber calculate reputation scores, and I believe there’s a fundamental flaw in how historical ratings are treated. Uber calculates passenger ratings using the last 500 rated trips, regardless of when those trips occurred. In my case, I have 455 ratings, 426 of which are five stars (93.6%). My overall rating is 4.86. What bothers me isn’t the score itself, but the underlying methodology. A negative rating from five years ago can carry exactly the same weight as one received yesterday. And if you’re an infrequent user who hasn’t accumulated 500 ratings, that negative feedback could influence your reputation for years. This raises an interesting question: Should reputation systems measure your historical average, or should they attempt to represent who you are today? One possible solution is exponential time decay: Weight = 2^(-t/H) Where t is the age of the rating and H is a half-life, perhaps 12 months. Under that approach, a rating from one year ago would carry 50% of its original weight, and one from two years ago just 25%. Of course, this introduces other challenges. How do you prevent someone with a history of poor behaviour from simply waiting for their reputation to recover? How do you maintain statistical confidence for infrequent users? Would Bayesian smoothing or a minimum effective sample size help? There’s also a broader philosophical question around the right to be forgotten. Should digital reputation systems indefinitely preserve the consequences of historical assessments, particularly when those assessments are subjective and potentially no longer representative? I’m curious how others would approach this. * Is a rolling window of 500 ratings statistically defensible without considering time? * Would exponential decay produce a fairer and more predictive reputation score? * Should platforms expose both a lifetime rating and a recent-behaviour rating? * Are there better approaches already being used in other reputation systems? I’d be particularly interested in perspectives from people who’ve worked on marketplace ranking, trust and safety, or reputation algorithms. It seems like a relatively simple mathematical change, but one with potentially significant implications for fairness across digital platforms.

posts.title: Second Brain and Agent Maintenance Thoughts on AI Usage?
posts.text: I have been seeing tons of stuff about people developing 'second brains' as a data vault for their AI usage on X. I fully understand the ideology, in terms of storing data, reducing context, having a single pane to work off of, etc. The part I struggle with, is that as an employee, I feel like every time I create a workflow, recurring data-pull, etc., it feels as if I am creating an app that I have to maintain myself. When my organization is constantly changing permissions, MCP accessibility, and token usage, I am having to maintain the app as if I were a developer, updating the automations as time goes on. I am grateful that I am technical enough to do this, and could probably avoid much of this problem if I had better technical foresight, but for a non-technical employee this seems like a significant barrier to AI-success on a per-employee basis. Anybody else experience the same maintenance struggle? I have developed countless useful agents that just die off in my mind after a few days because I forget about them, and they break.

posts.title: Ask HN: If AI tools are so good, why isn't your bug backlog empty?
posts.text: A lot of people outside tech ask me if AI is going to replace programmers and I just think: if that were the case we should be running out of things to do The bug backlog should be empty and we've caught up to every feature request from PMs to the point that we are bottlenecked on the business side But that does not seem to be the case with my own company or most devs I talk to in the industry So what gives?

comments.text: I don't know if I'm doing something wrong but bug fixing with AI has always been a crapshoot. You can absolutely tell an agent to fix an issue, and it will fix that issue, but the vast majority of the time that solution will be by adding code to cover the specific symptom in the bug report. It rarely considers or recommends solutions that have tradeoffs that may change behavior but will eliminate an entire class of similar bugs. This is mostly a problem of agents not having the autonomy of managing an entire project and having the ability to make tradeoffs to increase simplicity or maintainability, but when given that autonomy no AI model I've used uses that privilege to write simpler, more maintainable code.
comments.author: frostiness

comments.text: All my solo project backlogs _are_ empty. For my team projects, I still need my teammates to review code, so that bottlenecks how quickly we can burn down the backlog. If I didn't need code review I would have the backlog burned down in weeks, but I'd create a bunch of outages in the process (we do catch things in code review!) Also, some of my solo projects are gamedev-related, and gamedev is also bottlenecked on actually playing your game to see if its fun :) but it is great to get out of a 2 hour playtest session with notes and have a new build in like 15 minutes with the feedback incorporated.

comments.text: If your team and product had a large backlog before thats not going to change. AI tools amplify whatever it is you do so if you've been ignoring bugs and focusing most of the time on new features, AI isn't going to magically change what a team is working on. On a technical level, take your average NullPointerException or the equivalent in whatever language you use. Ask AI to go fix it and it will sanely wrap or check for nulls in that piece of code. Ask a lead or senior engineer to fix it and they will (hopefully) start with "why is this data null? it shouldn't be" and then trace back through logs or data, try to recreate with a real scenario and not only fix that bug but find there's an unhandled scenario somewhere else in the code base. Someone could prompt the AI to expand further and do a root cause analysis but do you trust it to find things and fix them properly?

posts.text: I wanted to hear some good opinions on all things AI and how they transform the Software industry. I'm asking because I honestly don't know what to do: I can try to always keep up to date with newest technologies, best practices, but I'm only me; if the demand for SWEs and jobs falls to the floor, I'm not sure I'll always get a place at the table (i.e. land a job) and I'm wondering whether I should try to do something else in some other industry. The onramp for coding becoming easier means non-tech people finally have a cheaper way to try out business ideas for domains they're experts in. Many of those will succeed and will need to hire developers, massively increasing the demand. Coding becoming easier means many more people will jump in, reducing wages rapidly. While there might be some work available, it'll mostly be low paid. Now that one person can do the job of 5, 4/5 will be laid off and we'll all struggle to get work. Now that one person can do the job of 5, AND there will be an increased demand for more developers from more businesses popping up, we'll be paid a hell of a lot more for the value we can generate. The speed of code generation is going to catch up to us in the form of tech debt, and we'll see the outcome of that in 12 months as codebase development slows to a halt and AI can't deal with it. posts.title: Ask HN: Why no AI-led memory vulns in Python?
posts.text: Python usually means CPython, which means C. Most AI-led vulnerabilities lately have been memory mismanagement - what is keeping Python isolated if it is written in C?

comments.text: Well, it might just be a matter of time. We've already had serious issues in Ruby with both string case conversion ( https://verialabs.com/ruby2shell/ ) and the regex engine (e.g. https://www.ruby-lang.org/en/news/2026/10/23/regexp-fixes-fo... ). And there have been attempts at fuzzing Python that have found real issues, apparently just not on the same scale (e.g. https://github.com/Broyojo/python-formalization ). A couple of things I can think of: first, the model for interfacing to "compiled code" — both C extensions, and compiled Python bytecode — isn't expected to be secure anyway, and never has been. You can trivially wrap a garbage `bytes` in a `code` object, execute it and get a segfault; and you can trivially use the `ctypes` API to corrupt memory. Second, the normal use paths are well-tested and bottom out in an interpretation layer that isn't very well optimized because of how much dynamic nonsense it has to support (even beyond other languages in its class like Ruby). On the other hand, the bytecode format tends to change with almost every "minor" release (i.e. annually now). There's probably plenty of room for a mistake in that churn.

comments.text: A suite of high-dopamine games which use smart exercise bikes as the control interface. When playing Zwift, Rouvy, etc, I find that I get too competitive and ruin longer workouts by trying to keep up with or sprint past people who are much faster than me over long distances. This is bad for building stamina and endurance, but I get bored, and it's hard to fight boredom and physical strain both at once. I do not get bored sitting in front of Balatro, Raccoin, Tetris - anything with bright colours and satisfying noises and combos. The first finished prototype game is very simple: you sort coloured marbles. Higher watt output from the bike means marbles are blown, by wind, upwards as they roll across the screen. Lower watt output means they fall. Steady watt output means they move horizontally. Marble goes into correct hole -> satisfying noise. It rewards steady watt output over time, with minor adjustments, which is what I'm trying to work on right now. I was pretty amazed by how engaging I found it (total iPad baby brain). The miles really fly by - I get tired before I get bored. I think that next I'll either do a tower defence game, or a less-dopamine-rewarding game in the style of Kerbal Space Program. Taking your actual weight and watt output, putting a bike with wings into a physics engine, and the gameplay loop being unlocking increasingly large airplane pieces, and designing - then flying - increasingly ridiculous airborne bicycles seems like a compelling idea, though less good for fitness. The control surface being so limited - essentially one measurement which can either go up or down - is a really fun constraint for creativity.

comments.text: I worked at a sports company forever ago, and ever since then, I've wanted to build my own NBA scores + stats site. After a few false starts over the years, I have a new concept called Center Court that I'm so excited about. It's primary purpose is for live boxscores because all of the major sports sites have terrible UI/UX experiences. I always defaulted to ESPN.com but it's so slow and awful. Center Court is basically a bridge between espn.com (or nba.com) and more advanced stat focused sites that don't offer a good live experience. The technical implementation behind it is quite novel in this space too. Instead of storing computed statistics in a database, I store raw play by play payloads immutability and everything else is derived from those and can be trivially rebuilt so the event log is a derived cache of the payloads. Every stat on every page is a pure fold over the event log at request time; no derived number is stored. This enables some powerful features like being able to re-derive a game's entire state at any point of the game (or even a time range). Example game to try out: https://centercourtlive.com/game/0022600197 The site is meant to be extremely fast. It's all server-side rendered with progressive JS enhancements. URLs are immutable and cached behind a CDN. https://centercourtlive.com/

posts.title: Ask HN: What still makes you proud?
posts.text: Larry Wall, who created Perl, a terse but expressive language more popular a few decades ago, used to say programmers should have "laziness" so they will complete tasks without extra yak-shaving, "impatience" so that they get to a solution fast, and - surprisingly - "hubris" so that they would document and write up their solutions and package them so that they are proud of them. AI has certainly made it easy to be lazy or impatient. What do you do that still makes you proud?

comments.text: Delivering software that "just works". Before AI the focus was on making software that "just works" for other developers. Designing a system and it's interfaces where people from other teams could independently hook into. One example is this autonomous bulldozer where the control system was a bunch of spagetti. How do you manage multiple events, commands, sensor data from various locations? With some kind of ROS-like RTOS. But that takes a learning curve to learn all the ROS bloat. (I met one of the original middleware developers when I interviewed for a robotic tractor company and he's like "lol, we never use that".) Anyways, I applied some design patterns to the ROS spageti and ended up with a synchronized, multithreaded interface that the ML image people could understand, the controls people could use. Today, that would be done in 5 minutes. So, now I'm happily making real stuff "just work". Before it would have taken months to build up a sliding random linear network code error correction system. Especially because we were using an antiquated TI dsp chip. Now, in two weeks plus some debug time, Boom: Deployed, and our radio audio quality is nicely improved. Need to do parameter optimization for a product? Code up some CLI hooks, test harness, instruct the LLM to have at it. Autonomous over night work and Boom: multi-variable plots showing the tradeoffs as parameters are tweaked. It's different for sure, but still fun.

posts.text: 1. product isn't important, sales is important 2. infra isn't important, talent to build it is important 3. which stack you use to build the product isn't important, business taste is important 4. pushing employees isn't the fastest way to ship, building a process from learnings is much more efficient share your learnings below

comments.text: Sales is easy when you have a good product. Ever tried selling a cup of coffee? Lasagna? An iPhone, even a used one? Selling a bad product is very difficult. Many founders jump from never having sold anything to trying to sell bad products. They pick up a lot of bad habits and none of the fundamentals; this includes things like being sleazy/pushy salespeople. Sales is simple: Find people who need the product and explain how it solves the problem. PMF is about the right sales channel for your product. Whether you want marketing, sales, branding, or customer success, it depends on your channel. For tech, you have PMF when $1 mil ARR looks like a goal, not a fantasy. Most of the time though, if you can't get a sale, it's a product problem. Many people don't realize that if it looks vibe coded, it's practically unfinished – it's not a proper product. You used to need about a third of development time dedicated to polish; these days it may be closer to two-thirds. Have you ever tried selling a latte? The latte art matters. It's not all functionality and features.
